title: Laws of Motion and Frame Dynamics
short_intro: Newton's laws of motion establish the foundational framework relating the state of motion of a body to the net external force acting upon it. They govern classical mechanics in inertial reference frames and require modifications via pseudoforces in non-inertial frames.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Statement and application of Newton's three laws of motion, linear momentum conservation, impulse, equilibrium of concurrent forces, friction (static, kinetic, rolling), and motion of connected bodies on inclined planes.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Non-inertial reference frames, centrifugal and Coriolis forces, motion in accelerated frames, variable mass systems (rocket propulsion), and constrained motion using Lagrangian formulations where applicable.

prerequisites: Scalar and vector algebra, vector addition, and resolution of forces
Kinematics of particles including displacement, velocity, and acceleration
Calculus: differentiation and integration of vectors with respect to time

concept_notes.heading: Newton's First Law and Inertial Frames
bullets: Defines inertial reference frames as frames in which bodies obey the law of inertia (zero net force implies zero acceleration).
Establishes the qualitative definition of mass as a measure of inertia.
Non-inertial frames are accelerated with respect to inertial frames and require fictitious forces for the application of Newton's laws.

concept_notes.heading: Newton's Second Law and Momentum
bullets: Defines linear momentum as p = mv and states that the net external force equals the time rate of change of linear momentum.
For constant mass systems, reduces to the vector equation F = ma.
Independent components principle: forces acting along orthogonal axes can be resolved and treated separately.

concept_notes.heading: Newton's Third Law and Conservation of Momentum
bullets: For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction; forces always occur in mutual interaction pairs between two bodies.
Action and reaction forces act on different bodies, hence they do not cancel each other out.
Internal forces sum to zero in an isolated system, leading directly to the principle of conservation of linear momentum.

concept_notes.heading: Friction and Contact Forces
bullets: Static friction (f_s ≤ μ_s N) opposes impending relative motion and self-adjusts up to a maximum limit.
Kinetic friction (f_k = μ_k N) acts during relative sliding and is independent of the apparent contact area and sliding velocity over typical ranges.
Rolling resistance arises from micro-deformations at the contact interface and is significantly smaller than sliding friction.

derivations.title: Rocket Propulsion Equation (Variable Mass System)
derivations.conditions: A rocket moving in free space with exhaust velocity relative to the rocket denoted as v_e.
steps: Write the initial momentum of the rocket at time t: p(t) = m v.
Write the momentum of the system at time t + dt: p(t+dt) = (m + dm)(v + dv) + (-dm)(v - v_e), where dm is negative (mass expelled).
Equate the change in momentum dp = p(t+dt) - p(t) to the external impulse F_ext dt.
Neglect second-order infinitesimal terms like dm dv.
Simplify to obtain m(dv/dt) = v_e (-dm/dt) + F_ext.

derivations.title: Acceleration of a Body on an Inclined Plane with Friction
derivations.conditions: A block of mass m placed on a plane inclined at angle θ with coefficient of kinetic friction μ_k.
steps: Resolve gravitational force into components: mg sin(θ) parallel to the incline and mg cos(θ) perpendicular to the incline.
Equate normal reaction N to the perpendicular force component: N = mg cos(θ).
Express kinetic friction as f_k = μ_k N = μ_k mg cos(θ).
Apply Newton's second law along the incline: mg sin(θ) - f_k = ma.
Substitute f_k and solve for acceleration a.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Friction Force vs Applied Force Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot with applied force (F_app) on the x-axis and frictional force (f) on the y-axis, showing a linear rise up to static maximum, a sharp drop, and then a constant kinetic friction value.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Static friction increases linearly to balance applied force until f_s(max) is reached; once sliding starts, friction drops to a lower, nearly constant kinetic value.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Directly tested in conceptual MCQ items regarding the comparison between static and kinetic coefficients.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Atwood Machine Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic of two masses connected by a string passing over a fixed frictionless pulley, used to measure acceleration as a function of mass difference.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Verifies Newton's second law by demonstrating that acceleration is proportional to the net driving force divided by the total mass system.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Exam questions test formula recall for acceleration a = [(m_2 - m_1)/(m_1 + m_2)]g and string tension.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Force-Time Curve (Impulse)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A curve plotting force versus time during an impact, where the area under the curve represents the linear impulse.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The total momentum change equals the integrated area under the F-t curve, regardless of the force profile's complexity.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used for numerical evaluation of impact forces and collision impulses.

solved_numericals.question: A body of mass 2 kg is pulled up a smooth inclined plane of inclination 30 degrees with an acceleration of 2 m/s^2. Taking g = 10 m/s^2, find the applied force parallel to the incline.
solution_steps: Identify forces acting parallel to the incline: applied force F_app, and component of gravity mg sin(θ).
Write equation of motion: F_app - mg sin(θ) = ma.
Substitute values: m = 2 kg, g = 10 m/s^2, θ = 30 deg, a = 2 m/s^2.

solved_numericals.question: A block of mass 5 kg rests on a rough horizontal surface with coefficient of static friction 0.4. What is the minimum horizontal force required to start motion? (g = 9.8 m/s^2)
solution_steps: Calculate normal reaction N = mg = (5 kg)(9.8 m/s^2) = 49 N.
Calculate maximum static friction f_s(max) = μ_s N = (0.4)(49 N).
The minimum horizontal force to start motion must equal this maximum static friction.

solved_numericals.question: A rocket burns fuel at a constant rate of 10 kg/s with an exhaust velocity of 2000 m/s relative to the rocket. Calculate the thrust force exerted on the rocket.
solution_steps: Recall thrust force formula for variable mass: F_thrust = v_e |dm/dt|.
Substitute given values: v_e = 2000 m/s, dm/dt = 10 kg/s.

assumptions_and_limitations: Newton's laws are valid only in inertial frames of reference unless modified by fictitious forces in non-inertial frames.
Macroscopic objects are treated as point masses when internal rotational and vibrational degrees of freedom are negligible.
Classical mechanics breaks down at speeds approaching the speed of light, where relativistic mechanics must be applied.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Action and reaction forces cancel each other out so bodies cannot move.
common_misconceptions.correct: Action and reaction forces act on different bodies, so they never cancel each other.
common_misconceptions.why: Cancellation applies only to forces acting on the same single body.

common_misconceptions.correct: Friction opposes relative motion or impending relative motion between surfaces in contact.
common_misconceptions.why: In rolling motion or walking, static friction actually provides the forward propulsive force.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Centrifugal force is a real force acting outward on a body in circular motion.
common_misconceptions.correct: Centrifugal force is a fictitious force experienced only in a non-inertial rotating reference frame.
common_misconceptions.why: In an inertial frame, only the real inward centripetal force acts on the body.

quick_revision: Newton's first law defines inertial frames and inertia.
Net force equals the time rate of change of linear momentum.
Action-reaction pairs act on different objects simultaneously.
Static friction self-adjusts up to μ_s N; kinetic friction is constant at μ_k N.
Rocket thrust is given by the product of exhaust velocity and fuel burn rate.
Fictitious forces such as centrifugal and Coriolis forces arise in non-inertial frames.
